course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
title: Optimization, Vector Fields, Divergence, and Curl
sessionGoal: Students should be able to finish a basic optimization problem and interpret divergence/curl for vector fields.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Start with optimization: find where the first derivatives are zero, then check edges if the region is closed.
Then say: a vector field puts an arrow at every point.
Divergence measures source/sink behavior. Curl measures local rotation.
Do Problem 1 if students need optimization. Do Problems 2 and 3 if they need vector fields.
sayThisFirst: Optimization means finding highest and lowest values.
For interior points, set the first partial derivatives equal to zero.
If the region has a boundary, you must also check the boundary.
A vector field is a function whose output is a vector.
Divergence is expansion or compression. Curl is rotation.
boardPlan: Work one absolute extrema example on a rectangle.
If time allows, show the 3D curl formula with a clean example.
keyFormulas: For closed bounded regions: check interior points, edges, and corners.
commonMistakes: Only checking the interior critical point and forgetting the boundary.
Forgetting that divergence is a scalar.
Forgetting that 3D curl is a vector.
notationWarnings: For 2D fields, write \(F=[P,Q]\) before computing divergence or curl.
When checking absolute extrema, label interior, boundary, and corners separately.

problems.title: Absolute extrema on a rectangle
problems.studentPromptLatex: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-2x-4y\) on the rectangle \(0\le x\le3\), \(0\le y\le4\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: because the rectangle is closed and bounded, absolute max and min exist. We must check both the inside and the boundary.

drawInstructions: Write 'inside + edges + corners' as the checklist.
Label the minimum at (1,2) and the maximum at the corners (3,0) and (3,4).

walkthrough.label: Check the interior
walkthrough.latex: \[f_x=2x-2,\qquad f_y=2y-4.\] Set both equal to zero: \[2x-2=0\Rightarrow x=1,\qquad 2y-4=0\Rightarrow y=2.\] So the interior critical point is \((1,2)\).

walkthrough.label: Check the boundary idea
walkthrough.latex: Each edge gives a one-variable quadratic. Its lowest value is \(-4\) on \(x=0\) and \(-1\) on each other edge. All are above \(-5\), so \((1,2)\) is the absolute minimum.

walkthrough.label: Check the corners for the maximum
walkthrough.latex: \[f(0,0)=0,\quad f(3,0)=3,\quad f(0,4)=0,\quad f(3,4)=3.\] The largest value is \(3\).

commonMistakes: Stopping after finding \((1,2)\) and not checking the boundary.
Assuming corners are enough. For absolute extrema, edges can matter too.
Forgetting that a maximum can occur at more than one point.

problems.title: Divergence and curl in 2D
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(F(x,y)=[x^2y,xy^2]\). Find \(\operatorname{div}F\) and scalar curl \(Q_x-P_y\). Then evaluate both at \((1,2)\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: name the components first. P is the first component and Q is the second component.

drawInstructions: Draw a small grid of arrows near (1,2).
At (1,2), write div F = 8 and curl F = 3.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that 2D scalar curl is a number.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 8 for divergence and curl.

problems.title: Divergence and curl in 3D
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(F(x,y,z)=[xy,yz,zx]\). Find \(\operatorname{div}F\) and \(\nabla\times F\). Then evaluate both at \((1,-2,3)\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: in 3D, divergence is still one number, but curl becomes a vector.

drawInstructions: Draw a 3D coordinate box or axes.
Write div F as one scalar.
Write curl F as a vector with three components.
Emphasize that the curl vector gives the axis/direction of local rotation.

commonMistakes: Putting the components of curl in the wrong order.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 8 for 3D vector fields.

wrapUpQuestions: Why do absolute extrema problems require checking boundaries?
What does divergence measure in plain words?
What does curl measure in plain words?
qualityControlNotes: Checked optimization values: interior minimum -5 at (1,2); corner maximum 3 at (3,0) and (3,4).
Checked 2D divergence/curl: div=4xy, curl=y^2-x^2, values 8 and 3.
Checked 3D divergence/curl: div=x+y+z, curl=[-y,-z,-x], values 2 and [2,-3,-1].
Visual specs include exact points/values when possible.
reviewSummary: Session 18 is ready with checked optimization and vector field examples.

open.title: Highest, lowest, and how things flow
say: Two ideas today. First, finishing optimization: on a closed region, where are the very highest and lowest values? Second, vector fields: an arrow at every point, like wind on a weather map.
For vector fields we ask two questions at each point: is the flow spreading out (divergence), and is it spinning (curl)?

ask.q: Your function has no critical points inside a closed square. Can it still have a maximum on the square?
ask.a: Yes: on the boundary. That's why we always check the edges.

idea.title: A closed region traps the answer
say: On a closed, bounded region, a continuous function always has an absolute max and min. They can only hide in two places: at interior critical points or somewhere on the boundary.
So the method is a checklist: find interior critical points, then turn each edge into a one-variable problem, then check the corners. Compare every candidate value, and the biggest and smallest win.
Nothing clever, just complete. The only real slip is skipping a place to look.
draw: Draw the rectangle 0 ≤ x ≤ 3, 0 ≤ y ≤ 4 with its four corners circled.
Write the checklist beside it: 1. inside (∇f = 0), 2. each edge (one variable), 3. corners, 4. compare.
Leave a table for the candidate values: point | f.

ask.q: On the edge x = 0, how many variables does f have?
ask.a: One: y. It becomes an ordinary single-variable problem.
They're the endpoints of each edge's one-variable problem.

launch.say: Find the absolute max and min of f on the rectangle. Work the checklist: inside, edges, corners.
circulate: Is anyone stopping at (1, 2)? Push them to the boundary.
Suggest splitting the edge work: each table takes one edge.
Look for someone who completes the square; have them share the picture.

askFirst.q: Why are we guaranteed an absolute max and min here?
askFirst.a: f is continuous and the rectangle is closed and bounded.

steps.say: Inside: f_x = 2x − 2 and f_y = 2y − 4 are both zero at (1, 2).

ask.a: Yes: 0 < 1 < 3 and 0 < 2 < 4. A critical point outside the region would be thrown away.
Not until we've checked the boundary.

steps.say: Each edge is a one-variable quadratic. Their lowest values are −4 on x = 0 and −1 on each of the other three edges, all above −5.

ask.q: On x = 0, what is f as a function of y?
ask.a: y² − 4y, lowest at y = 2 with value −4.

steps.why: Completing the square shows f = (x − 1)² + (y − 2)² − 5: squared distance from (1, 2), minus 5. The closest point is (1, 2) itself.

steps.say: Corners: 0, 3, 0, 3. The maximum is 3, at both (3, 0) and (3, 4).

ask.q: Using the distance picture, why these two corners?
ask.a: They're the farthest points of the rectangle from (1, 2), each √8 away: 8 − 5 = 3.

si18-p1.meaning: f measures squared distance from (1, 2), shifted down by 5. Its lowest point is the center (1, 2), and its highest points are the corners farthest from that center.

ifStuck.then: ask where the maximum is. It can't be at (1, 2), so it must be on the boundary.

si18-p1.transition: Switching topics: a vector field puts an arrow at every point. Divergence asks 'is it spreading out here?', curl asks 'is it spinning here?'.

launch.say: Find div F and the scalar curl, then evaluate both at (1, 2).
circulate: Divergence pairs P with x and Q with y.
Curl crosses them: Q with x, P with y, and the order matters.

askFirst.q: Picture water flowing out of a faucet onto a floor. Positive or negative divergence at the faucet?
askFirst.a: Positive: flow spreads out from a source.

ask.a: Every formula refers to P and Q; naming them prevents mixing them up.
Near (1, 2), more flow leaves a small circle than enters: a source.

steps.say: Curl = Q_x − P_y = y² − x². At (1, 2): 4 − 1 = 3.

ask.q: Which way does a tiny paddle wheel at (1, 2) spin?
ask.a: Counterclockwise, since the curl is positive.

steps.why: Q_x − P_y compares how the flow's sideways push changes across the paddle wheel.

si18-p2.meaning: At (1, 2) the flow is spreading out (div 8) and spinning counterclockwise (curl 3) at the same time.

ifStuck.if: a student uses P_y + Q_x for divergence
ifStuck.then: remind them divergence matches each component with its own variable: P with x, Q with y.

si18-p2.transition: In 3D, divergence is still a number, but curl becomes a vector: the axis the flow spins around.

launch.say: Find div F and curl F for the 3D field, then evaluate at (1, −2, 3).
circulate: Check div is a scalar and curl is a vector.
Walk the curl formula slowly: R_y − Q_z first.

askFirst.q: Which one is a vector in 3D: div or curl?

ask.q: Is the flow a source or a sink at that point?

steps.say: Curl: R_y − Q_z = 0 − y, P_z − R_x = 0 − z, Q_x − P_y = 0 − x. So ∇ × F = [−y, −z, −x].

ask.a: It's a cross product of ∇ = (∂x, ∂y, ∂z) with F: a 3 × 3 determinant with i, j, k on top.

steps.why: The third component, Q_x − P_y, is exactly the 2D curl from the last problem.

ask.q: What does this vector tell you?
ask.a: The axis the flow spins around near that point, with its length measuring how fast.

si18-p3.meaning: Near (1, −2, 3) the flow spreads out a little and spins around the axis [2, −3, −1].

ifStuck.if: a student mixes up the order of curl components
ifStuck.then: write the determinant with i, j, k on top and expand; the order falls out.

wrap.write: Absolute extrema: inside + edges + corners, then compare. div F = spreading out (a number). curl F = spinning (a number in 2D, a vector in 3D).

exit.a: Absolute extrema on a closed region can sit on the edge, where ∇f need not be 0.
How much the flow spreads out (or piles up) at a point.
How much, and around which axis, the flow spins at a point.
